en: The Jātaka:
The Ninth Chapter, The Section on Vultures (Gijjhavagga)
2. The Kosalambiya Jātaka:
“The populace is making a great noise;
do not think that anyone here is a fool.”
When the Saṅgha was being split,
they thought of nothing else; deluded,
though appearing wise, they did not consider what was superior.
Those who speak of what lies beyond the range of speech,
and who extend their mouths as far as they desire—
those wise ones do not follow that which leads them astray.
"He has struck me, he has hurt me,
he has defeated me, he has taken away what is mine"—
those who harbor such thoughts toward him, [are themselves overcome].
The truth does not satisfy them:
"He abused me, he struck me,
he defeated me, he robbed me."
But those who do not harbor resentment toward them—
for them, enmity subsides. For by enmity, enmities are never stilled.
They are never appeased here by hatred;
it is by non-hatred that they are appeased—
this is the eternal law.
But others do not understand that we are striving here;
yet those who truly understand it there—
Then disputes are stilled:
those who break bones, those who take life,
and those who seize cattle, horses, and wealth.
Even for those plundering a kingdom there is harmony; why should it not be so for you?
If one should find a prudent companion,
a wise and steadfast person who dwells in virtue, walking together with him,
having overcome all perils—
One should practice with a mind at ease and full of mindfulness.
But if one does not find a prudent companion to walk with— one who is virtuous,
wise, and lives a noble life— then one should rather wander alone.
Having abandoned his conquered kingdom like a king,
one should wander alone like an elephant in the forest;
wandering alone is better.
"There is no companionship with fools;
one should wander alone and commit no evil deeds,
free from anxiety like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest."
The Kosambiya Jātaka, the second.
